extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians, astronomers, and natural philosophers (readers of Newton's Principia)
extracted.subtask_description: A historical methodological procedure (Prop. XLII, Prob. XXI) for correcting a comet trajectory that was originally found graphically: pick three widely spaced observations, compute true positions in an assumed plane, compute sector areas and times, perturb node and inclination, solve linear relations to obtain corrected orbital elements (latus rectum, transverse axis, period).

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedure: correcting a graphically determined comet trajectory (Prop. XLII, Prob. XXI)
rubrics_metrics.description: A three-stage algorithm to correct a cometary orbit initially assumed in a plane: (Oper. 1) assume a plane of the trajectory found graphically, choose three comet positions defined by accurate observations as widely separated as possible; let A be time between first & second observations and B between second & third. Compute the three true positions in the assumed plane by trigonometric operations; then, about the Sun, describe the conic section through those true positions and compute the two sector areas D (between first & second) and E (between second & third). Let T be the total time the body would take to sweep area D+E at the comet's velocity (via Prop. XVI, Lib. I). (Oper. 2) Increase the longitude of the nodes of the assumed plane by +20' or +30' (call this P), keep the plane's inclination to the ecliptic, recompute the three true places in this new plane and the corresponding areas d and e and their total time t. (Oper. 3) Keep the node longitude from Oper. 1, increase the plane's inclination by +20' or +30' (call this Q), recompute true places and areas δ and ε and total time τ. Denote ratios C:1 = A:B, G:1 = D:E, g:1 = d:e, γ:1 = δ:ε and let S be the true time between first and third observations. Determine integers m and n (with observed signs) satisfying G - C = mG - mg + nG - nγ and T - S = mT - mt + nT - nτ. Then corrected inclination = I + nQ and corrected node longitude = K + mP (if I and K were inclination and node from Oper. 1). Using the corrections to the latus rectum and transverse axis from the three operations (R, r, ρ and reciprocals 1/L, 1/l, 1/λ), compute the true rectum and transverse axis by R + mr - mR + nρ - nR and 1/(L + ml - mL + nλ - nL). From the corrected transverse axis determine the comet's period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key practical points: (1) choose three observations as far apart as possible in time/space for sensitivity; (2) the prescribed perturbations (+20'–30') to node longitude and inclination are trial offsets to reveal dependence of computed sector times and areas on those parameters; (3) the method reduces to solving for small integer multipliers m,n that reconcile area/time ratios between the trial planes and the assumed plane; (4) final corrected orbital elements (latus rectum, transverse axis) follow by linear combination of the three sets of parameters; (5) this yields the comet's period. The text gives explicit notation and algebraic relations connecting observed sector areas/times to the corrections — implement exactly or follow equivalent algebraic linearization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observational principles and empirical regularities of comet tails
rubrics_metrics.description: A set of empirical laws about comet-tail appearance and motion: tails arise from the comet's head and extend into regions opposite the Sun; in planes of cometary orbits, tail directions deviate from exact opposition to the Sun in the sense of the head's forward motion along its orbit. To an observer placed in the orbital plane the tail appears directed away from the Sun; as the observer moves off that plane the deviation becomes more apparent and increases daily. The angle of deviation is smaller near the head and larger toward the tail's extremity; non-deviating tails appear straight while deviating ones curve, with greater curvature where deviation is larger and more observable where the tail is longer. The convex side of a curved tail faces the side from which deviation occurs, and many tails are brighter and have a sharper edge on their convex side than on the concave. Tails follow the motion of the head (not the celestial region where the head is seen), so they are not due to atmospheric refraction but originate from material supplied by the head.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observational diagnostics described: measure deviation angle as function of distance from head; note that curvature and brightness correlate with tail length and local density of vapors; tracking the geometry over time allows inferring when vapor at tail terminus began to ascend from the head (example chronology given: vapor at tail terminus on Jan 25 began ascending from head before Dec 11). Several historical comet sightings (e.g., 1680, 1668) are cited to illustrate changes in head brightness, tail length, and the appearance of tails when heads are near the Sun. Use these empirical rules to interpret tail geometry, estimate times of vapor ejection, and distinguish tail-origin hypotheses (e.g., head-ejected material vs. refractive phenomena).

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical hypotheses on the origin and dynamics of cometary tails
rubrics_metrics.description: Discussion and comparison of hypotheses for tail formation: (a) Kepler's idea attributing tail formation to action of solar rays carrying material outward; (b) the idea that particles levitate due to being extremely light and are carried away; (c) Newton's favored view that rarefaction (heating/rarefying of the cometary atmosphere by solar influence) causes the vapor to ascend from the head like smoke, the ascent being perpendicular if the head is stationary relative to the aether, or oblique if the head moves, and that the retained motion of the comet's head produces the observed oblique/curved tails. He notes that tails are composed of extremely rare vapor (far rarer than Earth's atmosphere) and that only very small amounts of matter are needed to produce the observed phenomena because cometary tails transmit starlight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical implications and critiques: Newton contrasts hypotheses by appealing to observed tail curvature, brightness distribution, and timing of ejections — favoring rarefaction/thermal ascent combined with retained orbital motion over simple radiation-pressure carrying of material. He also uses pressure/gravity and rarefaction estimates (comparison with Earth's atmospheric column) to argue that minute quantities of vapor suffice to produce visible tails and to propose that cometary vapors could contribute materially to planetary atmospheres and waters. When modeling tails, account for (i) the retained tangential velocity of ejected vapor, (ii) differential rarefaction and density across the tail column producing brightness asymmetries, and (iii) gravitational effects being insufficient to prevent tails and heads from adopting various relative positions observed.
